context.heading: Why refuse the king's food?
context.body: Patbag, a Persian loanword, means royal rations. The text never says exactly why Daniel refused them. Suggestions include meat not prepared by the Law (Leviticus 11), food first offered to Babylon's gods, or refusing to be bound to the king by eating at his table. Wine was not forbidden by the Law, which suggests more than clean and unclean was at stake.

context.heading: A new name
context.body: Daniel means "God is my judge". Belteshazzar probably calls on a Babylonian god to protect the king's life. Renaming claimed ownership and was meant to rewrite identity. Daniel answers to the new name for decades without ever forgetting whose he is.

context.heading: When was Daniel written?
context.body: Most evangelical scholars hold that Daniel's visions come from Daniel himself in the 6th century BC, as the book presents them, and Jesus refers to "Daniel the prophet" (Matthew 24:15). Many critical scholars date the finished book to about 165 BC, mainly because they doubt prophecy as detailed as chapter 11. Knowing both views helps when reading commentaries.

theology.title: God gave Judah up
theology.body: Babylon put the temple articles in its own god's treasury, which in the ancient world meant Babylon's god had won. Verse 2 insists otherwise: "the Lord delivered" Judah. Exile was God's judgment, not His defeat (2 Kings 24:3), and Jeremiah even calls Nebuchadnezzar "my servant" (Jeremiah 25:9).

theology.title: Faithful in a foreign city
theology.body: Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7). Daniel serves the empire well while keeping his heart for God, much like Joseph in Egypt. Peter calls Christians "exiles" too (1 Peter 2:11): fully present in the culture, never fully owned by it.

application.title: Pick the right line
application.body: Daniel accepted a new name, a new school and a royal job. He drew the line at one thing. Wisdom knows which battles actually decide who you belong to.
application.question: At work, which compromise is harmless and which would quietly change who you belong to?

application.title: Conviction with courtesy
application.body: Daniel did not stage a protest. He proposed a respectful ten-day test (v. 12) that protected the official who was responsible for him.
application.question: How could you hold your conviction this week without making an enemy of the person in charge?

application.title: Outlasting an empire
application.body: "Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus" (v. 21). He outlived the empire that captured him.
application.question: What would change if you measured faithfulness in decades instead of days?

context.heading: Not dwelling with mortals
context.body: The "astrologers" are kasdai, Chaldeans, a name for Babylonians that also came to mean their class of trained diviners. They protest that only the gods could do what the king asks, "whose dwelling is not with mortals" (v. 11). They are more right than they know, and they set up Daniel's answer.

context.heading: A stone not cut by hands
context.body: An even ("stone") cut out "not by human hands" smashes the statue and grows into a mountain filling the earth. Jesus calls Himself the rejected stone of Psalm 118:22 and warns that the stone will crush those it falls on (Luke 20:17–18), echoing this chapter.

context.heading: Which four kingdoms?
context.body: The head is Babylon (v. 38). The traditional Christian reading takes the rest as Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, with the stone as Christ's kingdom, begun at His first coming and completed at His return. Many others read Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece. Both readings agree that God's kingdom outlasts them all.

theology.title: The God who reveals
theology.body: The diviners said the gods do not live among people. Daniel's prayer praises the God who "changes the times", "removes kings" and "reveals the deep things" (vv. 21–22). Israel's God speaks, and in Jesus He came to dwell among mortals (John 1:14).

theology.title: A kingdom no one built
theology.body: Every empire in the statue was made by human hands; God's kingdom is not. Jesus opened His preaching with "The kingdom of God is near" (Mark 1:15), and Revelation 11:15 looks to the day when the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord.

application.title: Call your friends first
application.body: Facing execution, Daniel went home and asked his three friends to pray (vv. 17–18) before he went back to the king.
application.question: When the pressure is real, who do you call, and do you call them before or after you panic?

application.title: Refuse the credit
application.body: Daniel told the most powerful man on earth that the answer came "not because I have more wisdom" (v. 30). He had every reason to take the credit and did not.
application.question: When you do something impressive at work, how quickly does the story become about you?

application.title: Feet of clay
application.body: The statue looked like gold and stood on iron mixed with clay. Every human power has a weak point.
application.question: Which company, politician or system are you treating as if it will last forever?

context.heading: Bowing as politics
context.body: Segid means to bow down or pay homage. When the music played, every official from every province had to fall down together. In the ancient world religion and political loyalty were one, so refusing was treason. Early Christians later faced the same test with incense offered to Caesar.

context.heading: But even if He does not
context.body: Hen la, "but if not" (v. 18), may be the bravest words in the chapter. The three are sure God is able to rescue them, but their obedience does not depend on Him doing it. Their trust is in God Himself, not in a guaranteed outcome.

context.heading: A fourth man in the fire
context.body: The king sees one who looks like "a son of the gods", in his own pagan wording, and later calls him God's angel (v. 28). Many Christians have seen here an appearance of the Son of God before His birth; others see an angel. Either way, God was in the fire with them.

theology.title: God in the furnace
theology.body: God did not keep His servants out of the fire. He met them in it, as He promised: "when you walk through the fire, you will not be burned" (Isaiah 43:2). That presence comes fully in Jesus, Immanuel, "God with us" (Matthew 1:23).

theology.title: Worship belongs to God alone
theology.body: The first commandments forbid bowing to any image (Exodus 20:3–5). Revelation 13:15 pictures another image whose refusers are put to death, showing this pressure will return. The three refuse to give a creature the honor that belongs to the Creator.

application.title: When everyone is bowing
application.body: A crowd of thousands went down at the sound of the music. Three stayed standing, and everyone could see them.
application.question: Where is the pressure to just do what everyone else is doing strongest for you right now?

application.title: Obedience without a guarantee
application.body: "Even if He does not" is a harder faith than "He will." It obeys God for who He is, not for what He delivers.
application.question: Would your obedience survive if God said no to what you are asking Him for?

application.title: Not even the smell of smoke
application.body: They came out with no singed hair and no smell of fire (v. 27). The fire touched only the ropes that bound them.
application.question: What fire are you sure will ruin you that God might bring you through, or even use to set you free?

context.heading: The great tree
context.body: An ilan ("tree") reaching heaven and sheltering birds and beasts was a common picture of a great king. Ezekiel used the same image for Assyria and Egypt (Ezekiel 31:3–14). Jesus may echo it when He says His kingdom starts as a mustard seed and grows into a tree where birds nest (Matthew 13:31–32).

context.heading: Sanity returned
context.body: "I looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored" (v. 34). Manda means knowledge or understanding. The order matters: looking up came first. Pride had made him less than human; humility made him himself again.

context.heading: Break away from your sins
context.body: Daniel urges the king to turn from his sins by doing right and "showing mercy to the oppressed" (v. 27). Ancient kings boasted of caring for the poor; Daniel asks Nebuchadnezzar to actually do it. Judgment came a full year later (v. 29), time enough to listen.

theology.title: The Most High rules
theology.body: The point is repeated three times: "the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind" (vv. 17, 25, 32). God raises and lowers rulers as He wills (Romans 13:1). When Herod accepted praise as a god, he was struck down (Acts 12:21–23).

theology.title: Judgment with a door left open
theology.body: The tree was cut down, but its stump was left in the ground (v. 15). Even God's judgment held out hope of restoration. The chapter ends with a pagan king praising the King of heaven, "able to humble those who walk in pride" (v. 37).

theology.title: Mercy for Jerusalem's conqueror
theology.body: The man who burned the temple is given a testimony in Scripture, in his own words. Whether it became lasting faith, the text does not say. But God pursued the destroyer of His city with warnings, patience and restoration, a mercy that reaches people we would write off (1 Timothy 1:15–16).

application.title: Rooftop pride
application.body: "Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built?" (v. 30). He was not wrong that he had built it; he was wrong about who gave him the power.
application.question: What achievement do you catch yourself admiring as if you built it alone?

application.title: A year of warnings
application.body: Nebuchadnezzar got a clear warning and twelve months of grace. Nothing bad happened, so he moved on.
application.question: What warning have you filed away simply because nothing bad has happened yet?

application.title: Hard truth, said with love
application.body: Daniel was alarmed and wished the dream were about the king's enemies (v. 19). He told the truth anyway, as someone who wanted the king's good.
application.question: Who needs hard truth from you, said by someone who clearly wants their good?

context.heading: Temple cups at a party
context.body: Belshazzar calls for the man ("vessels") taken from Jerusalem's temple (1:2) and uses them to toast gods of gold and silver. It was a deliberate insult to Israel's God, made while Persia's army was close at hand. "Father" here can mean ancestor or predecessor, a common use in the ancient Near East.

context.heading: You knew all this
context.body: Daniel's charge is blunt: "you have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this" (v. 22). Belshazzar had heard what happened to Nebuchadnezzar. His sin was not ignorance but ignoring what he knew.

context.heading: Weighed and found light
context.body: Teqal means "weighed". Scripture often pictures God testing hearts on scales (Job 31:6; Proverbs 16:2). The king who looked so heavy with power and wealth turned out to weigh almost nothing in God's balance.

theology.title: Precise judgment
theology.body: God "numbered" Belshazzar's kingdom and brought it to an end (v. 26). His judgment is exact, not random, and when it came it came quickly: "That very night" (v. 30). Jesus tells of a rich man who heard the same words: "this very night" (Luke 12:20).

theology.title: God is not mocked
theology.body: Belshazzar treated holy things as party props. Paul warns that God will not be mocked (Galatians 6:7). Revelation later uses fallen Babylon as a picture of every proud power that defies God (Revelation 18:2).

theology.title: The finger of God
theology.body: God's own finger once wrote the Ten Commandments on stone (Exodus 31:18). Now a hand writes judgment on a palace wall. The God who gave His law also holds people to account for despising Him, and no amount of royal power can erase what He writes.

application.title: Knowing is not enough
application.body: Belshazzar knew his grandfather's story and repeated his pride anyway. Information about someone else's fall does not change a heart.
application.question: What lesson from someone else's failure do you know well but are not actually applying?

application.title: Partying at the gates
application.body: Babylon partied while an enemy army stood near. Distraction feels like freedom until reality walks in.
application.question: What are you numbing with entertainment instead of facing?

application.title: Keep your gifts
application.body: Daniel told the king to keep his rewards (v. 17), then read the hard message anyway. His honesty was not for sale.
application.question: When has a reward tempted you to soften something you knew was true?

context.heading: Nothing but the law of his God
context.body: Daniel's rivals give up looking for corruption and decide the only charge possible must involve "the law of his God" (v. 5). Dat is a Persian word for law, used for both the king's law and God's. The chapter becomes a clash between two laws.

context.heading: A thirty-day decree
context.body: The esar ("decree") banned praying to any god or man except the king for thirty days. Persian kings were not normally worshiped as gods, so it was probably presented as a loyalty test that flattered the king. Darius signed it without seeing the trap.

context.heading: Kneeling, just as before
context.body: Daniel "got down on his knees" three times a day (compare Psalm 55:17), "just as he had done before." Berakh can mean to bless or to kneel. He did not stage a protest or hide; he simply kept the habit he already had.

theology.title: A sealed stone, an early visit
theology.body: Plotters seek an innocent man's death, a stone is sealed over the den, and at dawn someone rushes to see if he lives (vv. 17–20). Many Christians see a foreshadowing of Jesus' tomb (Matthew 27:66; 28:1). Daniel was spared death; Jesus went through it and rose.

theology.title: The living God
theology.body: A pagan king ends up proclaiming that Daniel's God is "the living God" whose kingdom "will never be destroyed" (v. 26). It echoes chapters 2 and 7: empires fall, but God's rule does not. Even Persia's decrees bend to His purposes.

theology.title: Rescue now, or rescue later
theology.body: Hebrews 11 praises those who "shut the mouths of lions" and, in the same breath, those who were killed for their faith (Hebrews 11:33–37). Daniel was rescued from death; others are rescued through it. God's faithfulness is certain either way, and chapter 12 promises resurrection.

application.title: Predictable faith
application.body: Daniel's enemies built their whole plan on his habits. They knew exactly when and where he would pray.
application.question: If someone tried to predict your week, would your prayer life make the list?

application.title: Only faith to accuse
application.body: His rivals searched his work and found nothing. The only thing they could attack was his devotion to God.
application.question: If coworkers combed through your work and your expense reports, what would they find besides your faith?

application.title: Flattery gets signatures
application.body: Darius was flattered into signing a law that trapped his best official. He spent a sleepless night regretting it.
application.question: What kind of flattery could get you to sign something you would later regret?

context.heading: Beasts from the sea
context.body: For Israel the sea stood for chaos. The empires rise from it as chevah ("beasts"), wild hybrids: a lion with wings, a bear, a four-headed leopard, a terrifying fourth creature. In contrast, God's kingdom comes through one "like a son of man", a kingdom with a human face, as humanity was meant to rule (Genesis 1:26–28).

context.heading: The Ancient of Days
context.body: Attiq means "ancient", aged. God appears with white hair on a throne of fire, the eternal Judge before whom thrones are set and books opened. In Revelation 1:14 the risen Jesus is described with the same white hair, sharing the Ancient of Days' glory.

context.heading: Time, times and half a time
context.body: Iddan means a set period. "A time, times and half a time" is usually read as three and a half years, a limited, cut-short period of persecution. Revelation reuses it (Revelation 12:14; 13:5). Readers apply it to Antiochus IV, a future antichrist, or symbolically to the church's whole age of suffering.

theology.title: Son of Man, suffering and enthroned
theology.body: Jesus took this title and joined it to suffering: "the Son of Man must suffer many things" (Mark 8:31) and "came to serve, and to give His life as a ransom" (Mark 10:45). The one who receives every nation's service first served. The throne comes by way of the cross.

theology.title: The saints receive the kingdom
theology.body: The kingdom is given to the Son of Man (v. 14) and also to "the saints of the Most High" (vv. 18, 27). Christ shares His reign with His people (2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 3:21). Christians differ on how and when this is fulfilled, but not on who wins.

theology.title: Reading the beasts
theology.body: Many Christians read the fourth beast as Rome and the little horn as a future enemy of God (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4). Others read the beasts as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, with the little horn as Antiochus IV. Some see a near fulfillment pointing to a final one.

application.title: The beasts look permanent
application.body: Every empire in Daniel's day looked unstoppable. In the vision, each one lasts only until the court sits.
application.question: Which headline today makes you feel like the beasts are winning?

application.title: Leave room for the court
application.body: "The court was seated, and the books were opened" (v. 10). Final justice belongs to God's courtroom, not your revenge.
application.question: What injustice are you trying to settle yourself that you could leave to the court that will sit?

application.title: Troubled and hopeful
application.body: Daniel saw the happy ending and still went pale (v. 28). Hope does not require pretending the present is fine.
application.question: How can you be honest about what troubles you in the news while still trusting how the story ends?

context.heading: Horns and kings
context.body: Qeren ("horn") was a symbol of strength and royal power. The goat's great horn breaks "at the height of its power" (v. 8), a fitting picture of Alexander the Great, who died at 32. Four horns rise in its place, matching the generals who divided his empire.

context.heading: The daily sacrifice stopped
context.body: Tamid means "continual", the regular morning and evening offering (Exodus 29:38–42). Ending it cut off Israel's daily meeting with God. Antiochus IV banned it in 167 BC. The 2300 "evenings and mornings" may mean 2300 days or 1150 days of paired offerings, and both fit his era roughly.

context.heading: The time of the end
context.body: Gabriel says the vision concerns "the time of the end" (v. 17) and "the appointed time" (v. 19). Qets here may mean the end of this specific period of wrath rather than the end of the world. Many evangelicals see Antiochus as a preview of a final enemy (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4).

theology.title: History is not random
theology.body: Persia and Greece are named before Greece was a world power (vv. 20–21). God is not guessing about the future; He governs it. "I declare the end from the beginning" (Isaiah 46:10).

theology.title: Evil has an expiration date
theology.body: The little horn exalts itself even against "the Prince of princes", yet "he will be broken off, but not by human hands" (v. 25). Antiochus died in 164 BC on campaign in the east, of illness. God sets limits on every persecutor.

theology.title: An attack on the Prince
theology.body: The little horn attacks the temple and God's people, and in doing so it rises against "the Prince of the host" (v. 11) and "the Prince of princes" (v. 25). To persecute God's people is to oppose God Himself, as the risen Jesus told Saul: "why do you persecute Me?" (Acts 9:4).

application.title: Strong at the peak
application.body: The great horn broke at the height of its strength. Peak moments are where pride does its quiet work.
application.question: Where are you most confident right now, and how would you know if it had turned into pride?

application.title: Back to work
application.body: Daniel was ill for days after the vision, "then I got up and went about the king's business" (v. 27). He carried heavy truth into an ordinary job.
application.question: What heavy thing do you need to carry into tomorrow's ordinary work instead of waiting until you feel ready?

application.title: When deceit prospers
application.body: The horn "will cause deceit to prosper" (v. 25), for a while. Watching liars win is one of faith's oldest tests (Psalm 73).
application.question: Whose success through dishonesty are you tempted to envy?

context.heading: Reading Jeremiah's scroll
context.body: Daniel "understood from the sacred books". Jeremiah had promised return after seventy years when the people sought God with all their heart (Jeremiah 29:10–14). So Daniel seeks. He reads a promise and responds by praying it back to God.

context.heading: Seventy sevens
context.body: Shavua means "a seven". Most read seventy sevens as 490 years. It echoes the sabbath years: the exile repaid the land's missed sabbaths (2 Chronicles 36:21). Seventy years of exile opens onto seventy sevens, a far bigger restoration that deals with sin itself (v. 24).

context.heading: An anointed one cut off
context.body: Mashiach means "anointed one". Many Christians read verses 25–26 as Jesus, the Anointed One who is "cut off" in death, followed by Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70. Many critical scholars instead identify him with the high priest Onias III, murdered in 171 BC.

theology.title: How to read the seventy weeks
theology.body: Christians read verses 24–27 in several ways: as fulfilled in Jesus' ministry and death; as 69 weeks to Christ with the 70th still future, a final seven years; or as symbolic of the whole era until the end. All can agree on verse 24: atonement and everlasting righteousness, accomplished by Christ (Hebrews 9:26).

theology.title: Answered while still praying
theology.body: Gabriel arrives "while I was still praying" at the time of the evening sacrifice (v. 21) and says the answer went out "at the beginning of your petitions" (v. 23). God is not reluctant; He moves before we finish asking (Isaiah 65:24).

theology.title: Confession with we
theology.body: Daniel had been faithful for decades, yet he prays "we have sinned" (v. 5). He stands with his people under judgment, a faint picture of the sinless Christ who identified with sinners (2 Corinthians 5:21).

application.title: Read, then pray
application.body: Daniel read a promise and it changed his prayers. Bible reading that never shapes what we ask for stays theory.
application.question: When you read a promise in Scripture, how often does it change what you actually ask God for?

application.title: Stop saying they
application.body: Daniel included himself in the nation's sin. It is easy to confess the failures of our church, family or country as if we were watching from outside.
application.question: Where do you need to stop saying "they" and start saying "we"?

application.title: No résumé in prayer
application.body: "Not because of our righteousness" (v. 18). Daniel brought no record of good behavior, only God's compassion and His name.
application.question: What are you quietly asking God for on the basis of your own track record?

context.heading: A man dressed in linen
context.body: Daniel sees a figure in bad ("linen"), like a priest, with a gold belt and a face like lightning. Revelation 1:13–15 describes the risen Jesus in very similar terms. Some see an appearance of Christ here; others a high angel, perhaps Gabriel, since he needs Michael's help (v. 13).

context.heading: A great conflict
context.body: The message concerned tsava gadol (v. 1), a "great conflict" or hard service. Tsava is the word behind "LORD of hosts", God of armies. Daniel is being told that what lies ahead for his people is a long war, seen and unseen.

context.heading: Strengthened by a touch
context.body: Three times Daniel is touched and lifted (vv. 10, 16, 18), and he is told "be strong". Chazaq ("strengthen") returns in chapter 11 for proud kings making themselves strong. True strength here is received, not seized.

theology.title: Unseen battles are real
theology.body: The "prince of Persia" points to spiritual powers behind the nations. Paul says our struggle is "against the rulers... against the spiritual forces of evil" (Ephesians 6:12). Scripture gives few details, and wisdom stays within what it says. God's sovereignty does not make the conflict unreal.

theology.title: Heard on day one
theology.body: "From the first day... your words were heard" (v. 12). The answer took three weeks to arrive, but the delay was not God's indifference. Delay is not denial, and God's love for Daniel frames the whole vision.

theology.title: A gentle hand
theology.body: The heavenly figure is overwhelming, yet he touches Daniel, speaks peace and tells him not to fear (v. 19). John has the same experience when the risen Jesus lays His right hand on him and says, "Do not be afraid" (Revelation 1:17). God's holiness never cancels His tenderness.

application.title: Delay is not silence
application.body: Daniel's prayer was heard on the first day; he only learned that on day twenty-one.
application.question: What prayer have you assumed was ignored simply because the answer is slow?

application.title: Strength over speculation
application.body: This chapter can feed endless guessing about territorial spirits. The angel's actual message was simple: peace, be strong.
application.question: What would being strong look like this week if you stopped trying to map every unseen detail?

application.title: Start with treasured
application.body: Before any hard news, Daniel heard that God treasured him (vv. 11, 19). Fear shrank after that.
application.question: How would you face your hardest conversation this week if you believed God treasured you?

context.heading: Ships of Kittim
context.body: Kittim first meant Cyprus, then western peoples generally. In 168 BC a Roman envoy drew a circle in the sand around Antiochus IV near Alexandria and demanded an answer before he stepped out. Humiliated, Antiochus withdrew from Egypt and took out his fury on Jerusalem (v. 30).

context.heading: The abomination of desolation
context.body: Shiqquts means something detestable, usually an idol. In December 167 BC Antiochus set up pagan worship on the temple altar (1 Maccabees 1:54). Two centuries later, Jesus spoke of "the abomination of desolation" as still to come (Matthew 24:15), pointing to Rome's destruction of the temple in AD 70 and, many believe, beyond.

context.heading: Why so detailed?
context.body: Verses 2–35 track history so closely that many critical scholars conclude the chapter was written around 165 BC as history in prophetic form. Most evangelicals hold that God revealed it in advance, as the book claims. Verses 40–45 do not match what is known of Antiochus' death, one reason many see a final figure there.

theology.title: Refined, not abandoned
theology.body: "Those with insight will instruct many" (v. 33), yet some of them fall, "so that they may be refined" (v. 35). Suffering does not mean God has lost control. He uses even persecution to purify His people (1 Peter 1:6–7).

theology.title: Arrogance has a deadline
theology.body: The king "will exalt and magnify himself above every god" (v. 36), and Paul uses this language for the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:4). Yet he succeeds only "until the time of wrath is completed". Even the proudest rulers work inside limits God has set.

application.title: Flattery is a weapon
application.body: Antiochus won people over with flattery, and many joined the faithful "insincerely" (v. 34). Not every compliment or ally is safe.
application.question: Whose flattery do you need to treat with more suspicion?

application.title: Teach while it costs
application.body: The wise kept instructing others even as some of them fell. Their teaching was not a hobby but a lifeline for their neighbors.
application.question: Who could you help understand the faith this year, even if it costs you something?

application.title: God in the footnotes
application.body: This chapter reads like a dense list of kings, marriages and battles, and God tracked every one. Nothing about your season is too tedious for Him.
application.question: Which dull season of your life might God be watching more closely than you think?

context.heading: Michael stands up
context.body: Mikhael, "the great prince who stands over your people" (v. 1), appears again in Jude 9 and Revelation 12:7. In the darkest distress, those "written in the book" are delivered, the same book of life seen in Exodus 32:32 and Revelation 20:12.

context.heading: Life or contempt
context.body: Some wake to everlasting life, others to deraon, "contempt" or abhorrence. The word appears elsewhere only in Isaiah 66:24, the final verse of Isaiah. Resurrection leads to judgment as well as joy, as Jesus taught (John 5:28–29).

context.heading: Seal the book
context.body: Chatam, "seal", meant closing and stamping a document to preserve it until the right time to open it. Daniel is told to seal his book (v. 4). Revelation reverses the order: "Do not seal up the words... for the time is near" (Revelation 22:10).

theology.title: Resurrection hope
theology.body: Daniel 12:2 is the clearest Old Testament promise that the dead will rise bodily. Jesus' resurrection is the "firstfruits" of that harvest (1 Corinthians 15:20). God's salvation includes the body, not just the soul.

theology.title: How long?
theology.body: The question "how long?" (v. 6) gets symbolic answers: a time, times and half a time, then 1,290 and 1,335 days (vv. 11–12). Christians differ on whether these point to Antiochus' era, a future end time, or both. The blessing is promised to whoever waits faithfully (v. 12).

theology.title: An allotted inheritance
theology.body: Daniel will rise "to your inheritance", literally your goral, your lot. The word recalls the land allotted to Israel's tribes. An exile who never went home is promised a share in God's final kingdom, the inheritance Peter calls "imperishable" (1 Peter 1:4).

application.title: Shine by leading others
application.body: Those who "lead many to righteousness" will shine like the stars (v. 3). Being a good example nearby is not the same as actually helping someone toward God.
application.question: Who are you actively helping toward God right now?

application.title: Go your way
application.body: Daniel never got all his questions answered. He was told twice to "go on your way" (vv. 9, 13).
application.question: Which unanswered end-times question do you need to set down so you can get on with faithfulness today?

application.title: Rest, then rise
application.body: Daniel's final word is personal: "You will rest, and will arise" (v. 13). Christian funerals stand on that sentence.
application.question: How does a promised bodily resurrection change how you grieve someone you have lost?
